re drawn, not copied: don't make a mask or stroke by reflecting,
  flipping, rotating or translating another mask's or stroke's coordinates.
  A reflection in water is painted as its own shape, not as

## What to read
notes/easel_guide.md; notes/studio_notes.md;
notes/research/friedrich_materials.md (his materials and method, sourced);
notes/research/trees.md (how trees are built) and
notes/research/oil_paint_physics.md as needed.

## Working
- You make every artistic decision.
- Friedrich's pictures are full of small, particular details; don't stop at broad
  passages.
- Look at your painting often, whole and close up.
- Keep a working journal with `bin/easel note "..."` as you go: your own
  working notes. Add to it; don't rewrite earlier entries.
- Develop the painting until you judge it complete. Then save it
  (`bin/easel save`) and close the session.

## When you're done
Reply with the paths of the saved painting and its log, the painting's
title if you give it one, and if you like a few sentences about the
picture.

` puts a round disc at every point, both ends included, so it
    reaches half a width past its end points.
47. Two separately softened masks that meet leave a light gap or a dark
    overlap along the seam. A mask and its inverse (`m` and `-m`) meet
    without one.
48. A passage bounded by a mask shows a cut edge wherever its paint differs
    from its neighbor's at the mask's edge.

## Drying and time

49. Paint goes from open (workable) to setting (stiff, barely blends) to
    tacky to touch-dry. Lead-white-rich paint gels in about 2 hours and
    average paint in about 3.5. A lean coat is touch-dry in about a day;
    bone black and lakes take days. Thick or oily paint dries slower.
50. `wait` ages every point of the canvas at once. Which passages have set
    depends on their pigment, thickness and oil, not on where you worked.
51. A long pass is painted in 15-minute slices that age
    between them, so its first part is older than its last. While the work
    goes on, the paint under a later passage is still open and comes up
    into it.

## Pencil

52. Graphite doesn't take on wet paint, and paint laid over it seals it.
    Thin paint lets a line show and body color hides it. Under a thin first
    layer a firm line reads as a thin dark line until a fuller layer covers
    it.

ons (strokes, touches, passes, trips to the palette) and
`wait(minutes)` advance it. Real time between commands does not: paint
doesn't dry while you think. `wait(minutes)` passes painting time at once;
it doesn't make you wait that many real minutes.

- **Hand time.** Every stroke, touch, pass and trip to the palette takes
  the time a hand takes to make it: a stroke by its length and the
  brush's width (broad sweeps are fast, fine lines slow per mm), a
  stipple touch about a third of a second, a dip into a pile on the
  palette 2.5 s, knifing a new pile 20 s. The paint ages while the hand
  works: a long pass is painted in slices of 15 minutes, and its first
  strokes are setting by the time the last go on.
- **`wait(minutes)`** lets time pass with your hand away from the canvas:
  minutes, hours or days (`wait(3 * 24 * 60)`), up to 10 years
  (5,259,600 minutes). It returns the time of day, e.g. `day 3, 14:20`
  (the painting was begun at 09:00 on day 1).
- **`drying(x, y)`** tells you what the paint there is like to the touch:
  `"open"` (workable: it blends and lifts), `"setting"` (stiff, barely
  blends), `"tacky"` (set; it grabs the brush) or `"dry"` (touch-dry).

Each film dries at its own pace, set by its pigments, its thickness and
its oil. Thin lean paint of fast-drying pigments is touch-dry in a day;
thick, oily paint of slow pigments can stay open for weeks. Wet paint
under a new stroke comes up into it; paint laid over dry paint sits on
top of it.

function postmill(x, base, H, rot, seed)
  local bw = 0.3*H
  local bTop, bBot = base - H*0.95, base - H*0.45
  -- trestle and post
  local r = brush{kind="rigger", width=0.7, point=1}
  r:reload(mP, 0.6)

  r:stroke({{x, bBot},{x, base}}, {pressure={0.7,0.7}})
  -- the body with its gabled roof
  local body = poly({{x-bw/2, bBot},{x-bw/2, bTop+0.08*H},{x, bTop-0.02*H},{x+bw/2, bTop+0.08*H},{x+bw/2, bBot}})
  work(body, {hand="detail", pile=mP, tool={kind="round", width=1, point=0.2}, angle=math.pi/2, coverage=3, fill=true, clip=true, seed=seed})
  work(body * rect(x-bw/2, bTop-2, bw*0.4, H), {hand="detail", pile=mL, tool={kind="round", width=0.8, point=0.2}, angle=math.pi/2, coverage=1.5, clip=true, seed=seed+1})
  -- four sails from the hub on the front of the body
  local hx, hy = x - 0.05*H, bTop + 0.15*H
  local R = 0.62*H
  for k=0,3 do
    local a = rot + k*math.pi/2
    local ca, sa = math.cos(a), math.sin(a)
    r:reload(mP, 0.6)
    r:stroke({{hx, hy},{hx + ca*R, hy + sa*R}}, {pressure={0.55,0.45}})
    -- the lattice frame as a narrow blade along the outer part
    local px, py = -sa, ca
    local w = 0.09*H
    local blade = poly({{hx+ca*R*0.25, hy+sa*R*0.25},{hx+ca*R, hy+sa*R},{hx+ca*R+px*w, hy+sa*R+py*w},{hx+ca*R*0.25+px*w, hy+sa*R*0.25+py*w}})
    work(blade, {hand="detail", pile=mP, tool={kind="round", width=0.7, point=0.3}, angle=a, coverage=1.3, clip=true, seed=seed+2+k})
  end
end

el), `eye`, `fov`, `ground` (a function
`(X, Z)` giving the surface's height in meters; flat by default), `water`
(`{level=, ripple=}`: a level reflecting surface), `sun` (`{azimuth=,
elevation=}` in degrees: the light's direction; azimuth 0 is straight
ahead, -90 to the left, 180 behind you), `visibility` and `backdrop`.
With water, `v:water()` and `v:mirror(x, y)` say where it is seen and
what it reflects; `v:land()` and `v:sky()` are where the surface and the
space above it are seen. `w:proxy(s, body)` places a body that casts a
shadow but isn't seen. `w:aerial(Z)` and `aerial(dist, visibility)` give
how much air lies between the eye and a distance (0..1).

**Depth.** A view knows what lies behind what. `w = w:layer(name, mask,
depth)` registers a shape you paint by hand at a depth (meters, a spot, a
canvas point `{x, y}` where it stands on the ground, or `"ground"`); make
the view after it. Then `v:visible(x)`, `v:front(x)`, `v:behind(x)`,
`v:at_depth(m)`, `v:between(a, b)` and `v:seen(x, y)` are masks and
answers, and `v:cast_shadow{soft=, from=}` and `v:contact_shadow{reach=,
from=}` are shadows that fall off with distance from what casts them.
Things are named by body number, layer name, `"ground"`, `"water"`,
`"surface"`, `"sky"`, `"bodies"`, `"layers"`, a mask or a list. Passes take
`visible=` (only where that is seen), `behind=` (only where nothing in
front of it is) and `at=` (a depth in meters): strokes still overrun the
mask's own edges, never what is in front.

The first chunk is `canvas{}`. When the painting is done, `bin/easel save`
writes the picture to `out/easel/painting/painting.png`; the program that
paints it is `paintings/lua/painting.lua`.

In the examples below, `<tube>` stands for a name from the tube box and
`<parts>` for a number of parts you choose.

## The canvas

```lua
canvas{size=400, aspect=1.25, linen={16, 14}, seed=1,
       ground={{pile={{"<tube>", <parts>}, {"<tube>", <parts>}}, um=100, apply="knife", texture=0.3},
               {pile={{"<tube>", <parts>}}, um=50, apply="brush"}}}
```

- `size`: the canvas's width in mm (50 to 5000).
- `aspect`: width / height.
- `linen`: plain-weave linen, threads per cm, one number or `{warp, weft}`
  (4 to 60).
- `ground`: the preparation layers, bottom first. Each is a paste mixed
  from tubes in parts (as a pile is, below), a thickness in µm (5 to 400)
  and how it is put on: `"knife"` (levels the weave; `texture` 0..1 is the
  knife's waviness), `"roller"` (a fine even texture) or `"brush"` (laid in
  crossing strokes, its striations stay). The ground is dry when painting
  starts.
- `seed`: the randomness of the linen, the ground and everything after.

It sets `W` (1000) and `H` (`1000 / aspect`). The canvas is always 1000
units wide, whatever its pixel width. The origin `(0, 0)` is the upper
left corner; x increases to the right and y downward. Angles are radians,
0 left to right, π/2 downward.

Widths are in canvas units. A brush keeps its paint across strokes and
chunks, so strokes from one load run dry, and a brush that has been
through wet paint carries some of it. Pressure ranges from 0 (lifted)
to 1 (fully pressed); a stroke's `pressure` is `{start, end}`.
`ramps` gives the press-down and lift-off fractions, `swell` pressure factors
along the stroke, `orient` `"across"`, `"along"` or a fixed angle.

Brushes are blunt unless given a `point` (0 blunt, 1 a full point). A
pointed round or rigger lays a hairline at light pressure and spreads to
its belly when pressed, so its width follows the pressure and a stroke
whose pressure falls to 0 ends in a point.

`io`, `os`, `debug`, `require`, `dofile`, `loadfile`
  and `collectgarbage` aren't there. `print` goes to the reply.
- **Lua 5.5.** Numbers are integers or floats (`7 // 2` is 3, `7 / 2` is
  3.5). Bitwise operators are built in; there is no `unpack` (use
  `table.unpack`). Loop variables are read-only. Don't write `global`
  declarations (one switches its chunk to strict mode).
- **`pairs` walks a table in the same order in every session and replay.**
  Tables keyed by strings, numbers and booleans walk in Lua's order; a
  table with any other key walks in a fixed order (booleans, numbers,
  strings, then other keys in the order they were made). For a big list,
  `ipairs` is faster.
- **Memory.** A mask costs 4 bytes a pixel, a form 28. Keep big things
  `local` when later chunks don't need them.

## The journal

`notes/journal.md` is your working journal. `bin/easel note '<text>'` (or
`bin/easel note -` to read the text from stdin) appends an entry stamped
with the session's painting time, such as `day 2, 09:40`; the session must
be open. Entries already there stay as they were written; writing a note
doesn't advance painting time.

the live canvas. The log, `paintings/lua/painting.lua`, is plain Lua with
a line `--@ chunk N` before each chunk. The easel keeps a record of it in
`out/easel/painting/committed.lua`. If the log is changed, shortened or
missing, the easel refuses to continue.

I'm thinking about how Friedrich renders oak foliage as clustered, irregular masses with ragged silhouettes rather than individual leaves, so I plan to group the 25 smaller clumps into roughly six larger irregular masses to capture that layered, jagged look.

I want to fill the sky gaps within each mass with dark-mid foliage while leaving a few irregular holes between masses, then light each mass from top-left with shading below, and scatter small leaf-cluster touches at the edges — keeping some branches visible through the gaps rather than covering everything. I'll define the masses using a morphological closing operation on the clump silhouette to merge nearby clusters, then hand-carve a few sky holes with roughened edges, and paint the newly closed regions with foliage while adding noise to the overall silhouette edge so it doesn't read as smooth.

Rather than lighting each ball individually, I'll reorganize the lighting at the mass level by defining six large flattened ellipsoids that establish top-left highlights and underside shadows across each mass, layering this over the existing ball-lit pattern with dense stipple work to reconcile the values. I'm working out the crown extents and grouping the clumps into horizontal tiers — a top mass, left-upper mass, right-upper mass — each with its own center point and radius to guide this layered lighting approach.

I'm continuing to define the remaining masses (left-mid, center, right-lower) by grouping clumps into their centers, while also making sure to preserve the sky holes between the masses, like the existing gap around canvas coordinates (290,190), accounting for the crop scale and origin offset.

Rather than manually selecting each hole, I'm thinking it's simpler to apply a moderate closing operation so small gaps fill in while larger ones remain open, then hand-add a few holes afterward. I'm checking distances between neighboring circles to see where gaps are actually touching versus genuinely open, using radius sums to confirm overlap.

The bigger issue is that each ball currently reads as individually lit with its own highlight and shadow, which is what creates the broccoli texture — to fix this I'd need to essentially repaint the crown by stippling darker tones over many of those highlights and adding light to some shadowed areas to consolidate everything into larger, cohesive light and dark masses. This is a substantial repaint but feasible with a stippling technique that keeps texture on a dry layer. I'm also considering whether a full silhouette repaint of the crown might be necessary, since the individual ball outlines against the sky are the most obvious giveaway of the broccoli look.

I'm thinking of drawing inspiration from Friedrich's gnarled tree style, with foliage clumps hanging off visible limbs and more sky breaking through, rather than a uniform ball-cluster silhouette — the main correction needed is varying the ball sizes and lighting rather than keeping them uniform. My plan is to close the original silhouette with a larger radius and rough, noise-driven edges to create an irregular leafy outline, then fill in the gap zone between the old and new silhouettes with additional foliage detail.

Then I'm layering in tonal massing: about seven flattened ellipsoid masses lit from the upper-left, with darker stippled shadow where balls sit within mass shadow, soft mid-tone half-tones clustered on the lit side, small clustered highlights, and a light shadow pass on the crown's right side, finishing with lacy leaf sprays dragged along the edges for texture.

I still need to redo a few branches poking through gaps, and I want to preserve some of the existing sky holes between the foliage tiers rather than closing them all up — checking the image for where those horizontal gaps currently sit between tiers so I can keep them consistent.

Since I can't inspect the mask directly, I'll compute the closing operation and trust the result, spot-checking a few points. The lower limbs and trunk look fine as-is.

Turning to the cloud, it currently reads as a muddy pinkish-grey mass with a pale halo — I'm weighing whether to unify it with a thin warm glaze (previous attempts gave blotches) versus repainting it opaquely with cream-white lit tops.

I'm considering scumbling a pale opaque layer over the lit areas while wet, blending with a badger brush before it sets, though this tends to produce streaky results since blending only moves the fresh paint over the dry underlayer. The cloud's edge has a distinct lighter rim, roughly 10 units wide, that reads like a cutout — I could try matching it to the pale cream-blue sky tone nearby, though mismatched color was an issue before, so it's risky.

Rather than fix the halo, I think I'll add lit cream-white tops to the upper-left billows with a greyer underside, since the cloud currently sits at a uniform pinkish mid-value that lacks the contrast a cumulus needs against the sky — though Friedrich often keeps cloud masses darker than a luminous horizon, so this may be fine as is. Given that prior glazes have blotched, I'll set the cloud aside for now, treat the streaky close-up texture as acceptable since it reads fine from a distance, and shift focus to the oak.

Small additions like a flock of birds, some cows, or a path could round things out. Now I'll set up the scratch directory and start on the oak, beginning with the closing mask test.

- **The cloud:** I repainted it with a lit head at upper left and grey-violet shadow to the lower right.

- **Title:** *June Morning on the Meadows before the Town*

This is a wide summer morning on flat Pomeranian river meadows, with a low horizon and a sky running from deep cobalt at the top to warm cream at the horizon. On a grassy rise at the left stands a lone oak in full leaf, with one dead limb breaking out of its crown. Under it, a man in a dark coat and a woman in a wine-red dress stand with their backs to us, looking toward a Hanseatic town across the meadows. The town is a violet-grey silhouette: a tall hall church with a needle spire and a few other towers, set against a large summer cloud. A river of pale reflected sky winds toward the town between pollard willows.

The meadows are full of small scenes. On the left a shepherd leans on his crook beside his dog and flock. Haymakers load a wagon behind a bay horse among the hay cocks. Two horses graze, cattle stand by a fence along the ditch, and a barge with a red-brown sail heads up the river toward the town. There are field stones and buttercups in the near grass, and swifts high in the sky.

In this last session I added the barge, the flock with its shepherd and the hay wagon. I also removed the pale halos around the towers. Patching them locally only made ghostly spires, so I repainted the whole cloud and then glazed the town so it reads as a separate shape in front of the cloud.

Two weaknesses remain. The right side of the oak's crown is still a heavy, rather even dark. The cloud is soft rather than glowing, and streaky seen close up.

I'll keep the scope tight: for the right half of oakNew, I'll scatter roughly 20 small hand-placed ellipsoids as sub-clumps, then stipple the mid-tone color onto their lit tops at low coverage, clipped to a slightly shrunk crown mask. The river reflections and sky streaks I'll leave alone for now since they're acceptable as-is. Before touching anything, let me check the current drying state and look more closely at the right crown region.

events.text:
I've saved the painting as finished and closed the session.

- **Painting:** `[local path redacted]
- **Log:** `[local path redacted]
- **Title:** *June Morning on the Meadows before the Town*

A lone oak in full June leaf stands on a grassy rise at the left. Under it a couple, seen from behind, looks out over the river meadows toward a Hanseatic town. The town sits low on the horizon under a large summer cloud: a hall church with a needle spire, two more towers and a row of gabled houses. The silver river winds between pollard willows toward the town, with a barge under a red-brown sail. On the meadows, haymakers are loading a wagon among the hay cocks, a shepherd with his dog watches a flock of sheep, and two horses and three cattle graze by a post-and-rail fence. Buttercups, daisies and two weathered granite stones sit in the near grass. Post mills stand on the horizon and swifts fly high over the town. As in Friedrich, the sky takes most of the picture, and the figures are small and turned away.

In this session I made one change. The shaded right side of the oak's crown had been a single flat dark. I stippled a dull olive onto the tops of about twenty small leaf clusters there, so it now reads as foliage in shade and still balances the sunlit left side.

Some weaknesses remain: the cloud is soft rather than luminous, and it is streaky up close. The oak's leaf masses are still a little too round, and the willow reflections are rather blotchy. Taken as a whole, the picture holds together: the dark oak against the pale sky, the grey-violet town and cloud, and the river leading between them.

I didn't run `bin/easel check` to confirm that the log still replays to the same canvas, because a full replay takes about 25 minutes.
